title: Stay warm, cool and sheltered
short: Heat, cold, smoke, carbon monoxide, damaged homes and outdoor shelter
intro: Find guidance for keeping people at a safe temperature and under cover when the power is out, the air is smoky, or home is damaged or unsafe. It also points to safe heating and generator use, because the fixes people grab first can poison or burn them. For treating someone already ill from heat or cold, see the first-aid topic.

limits.text: Use generators and fuel only outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages; carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless and can kill.
Never use a gas stovetop, oven, grill or dryer to heat your home, and never leave a vehicle running in a garage, even with the door open.
If your carbon monoxide alarm sounds or you smell gas, move to fresh air immediately, call for help from there and stay until emergency personnel arrive.
Never use heaters designed for outdoor use inside; keep kerosene heaters ventilated, refuel them outside and keep them at least three feet from things that can burn.
Do not rely on electric fans when it is over 95°F outside: they can increase the risk of heat illness.
Heat stroke (very high temperature, red hot dry skin, confusion, unconsciousness): call 9-1-1 or get the person to a hospital immediately.
People on fluid-restricted diets (for example, with kidney disease) should consult their doctor before drinking more fluids in heat.
A body temperature below 95°F is an emergency.
Evacuate immediately if authorities tell you to. If trapped by wildfire, call 9-1-1 and give your location, but emergency response may be delayed or impossible.
People with asthma, COPD or other lung conditions should take precautions in poor air quality because it can worsen symptoms.
Do not enter a building with signs of structural damage, a gas smell, floodwater around it, or fire damage not yet inspected; have a qualified inspector check a damaged home.
If there are major cracks in the chimney or foundation, or the home has moved, get everyone out of the home.
If experts or local officials tell you to evacuate, leave. Older people and those with access and functional needs may need to leave well before official notice.
Living on higher floors of multistory buildings, and being confined to bed, are linked to a higher risk of heat-related death.
